title: Analog Layout Techniques
intro: Layout is part of circuit design in analog: the best schematic fails if its matched devices are placed badly.

items: Same orientation and shape: transistors that must match should be identical in W, L, direction and surrounding.
Common centroid: arrange devices A and B as A B B A (or A B / B A in 2-D) so linear process gradients cancel.
Interdigitation: split each device into fingers and interleave them.
Dummy devices at the ends of arrays so that edge devices see the same environment.
Symmetry in routing: equal length and equal coupling for differential signals.

blocks.text: Switching digital circuits inject noise into the shared substrate, which reaches analog devices through junction capacitances and the body terminals. Guard rings (grounded p+ rings around sensitive circuits), separate supply pins and distance reduce it. Deep n-wells can isolate NMOS devices.

A bond wire adds about 1 nH per mm of inductance and a few hundred fF pad capacitance. At GHz frequencies these parasitics matter: ground bounce on a shared bond wire, and resonances with pad capacitors. Flip-chip and multiple bond wires reduce the impedance.

blocks.title: Common-centroid
blocks.text: A linear gradient raises VTH by 1 mV per um across a row. Device A occupies positions 0 and 3 um, B positions 1 and 2 um (ABBA). Compare the average VTH shift of A and B with an AABB layout.
solution: ABBA: A averages (0 + 3)/2 = 1.5 um, B averages (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5 um: identical, so mismatch is zero.
AABB: A at (0 + 1)/2 = 0.5, B at (2 + 3)/2 = 2.5: a 2 mV difference.
blocks.answer: ABBA cancels the gradient; AABB leaves 2 mV.
